Great question! If you're interested in diving deeper into African cinema, there are some more gems you might want to consider. 

Firstly, 'Black Girl' is another powerful film from Ousmane Sembène that I'd recommend. It's gripping and intimate, and really delves into post-colonialism in a thoughtful way. 

In a more contemporary setting, 'Timbuktu,' directed by Abderrahmane Sissako, is a hauntingly beautiful film that explores some heavy themes. 

Another film that really resonated with me is 'The Battle of Algiers.' It's an Algerian production, directed by Gillo Pontecorvo. A gritty, visceral portrayal of the Algerian revolution, it's shot almost like a documentary which makes it all the more harrowing. 

Of course, every film you seek out is going to tell its own unique story that contributes to the vibrant and diverse tapestry of African cinema. Have fun with your exploration!

*Who Killed Captain Alex?* is a truly enjoyable movie with a backstory that can warm the coldest of hearts.

This movie was made by impoverished residents of a Ugandan ghetto on a budget of less than $100. It was edited on a computer that the director himself made out of scrounged spare parts. 

And, despite the filmmakers' complete lack of connections and resources, this film went viral online and has resonated with audiences around the world because of the sheer love of movies and joy in making movies evident in every scene. Amateurish in the very best way, in that word's original sense of 'done out of love'. If you ever got your friends together to make a movie when you were teenagers, you'll enjoy *Who Killed Captain Alex?*
